prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: a piano tuner who hears a note nobody played. Prose only, no headings.
text:
The rain tapped against the windowpane of Mr. Gable's shop in rhythmic intervals that matched his own internal metronome, usually set to 60 beats per minute. Inside, the air smelled of dust, old varnish, and the sharp, metallic tang of fine-tuning hammers. Elias was a man who had spent forty years listening to silence between notes, seeking the perfect pitch in instruments that rarely existed naturally. He moved through his apartment above the shop with the quiet efficiency of someone accustomed to small spaces and larger responsibilities; tonight, however, those responsibilities were purely auditory, and they kept him awake long after the streetlights outside flickered off one by one.

It began as a whisper, indistinguishable from the settling of floorboards or the groan of an aging radiator. Elias sat at his workbench, polishing a small screwdriver that looked more like surgical steel than a tool for tuning wire strings. The silence in the room was heavy, pressurized by the weight of expectation he carried every time he lifted a lid and prepared to hear something new. Then came it: a low C-sharp from the far end of his upright piano, which had been sitting empty for six months since its previous owner moved away. No one sat at that bench. Elias's hands froze mid-motion on the polishing rag. He stopped breathing, holding his breath until his lungs burned slightly, straining to isolate the source of the sound. It wasn't a trick of the rain; it was too clear, possessing a specific timbre that vibrated in his chest rather than just ringing in his ears.

He stood up slowly, knees cracking like dry twigs under decades of use, and walked toward the instrument. The room seemed to tilt slightly as he approached the keyboard, but when he reached out with a gloved hand, there was nothing on the bench. He turned back to face the keys again, squinting into the dim light pouring from his single reading lamp. His mind raced through familiar malfunctions—a sympathetic resonance caused by humidity swelling feltors in unexpected ways, or perhaps the acoustic coupling between two rooms if he lived near a neighbor with an unspeakable habit—but neither explained this clarity. The note hung there, suspended in the air like dust motes caught in a sunbeam that wasn't actually shining through any window.

He sat down and pressed his palm flat against the cold ivory keys of middle C-sharp, feeling no key depress beneath him. He reached for the sustain pedal anyway, just to test if it was stuck or warped by gravity alone, but even without touching anything else on the piano, the sound continued to bleed into the room. It wasn't a haunting melody; there were no melodies in single notes unless context gave them one, and this note had none except its own persistent existence. Elias tried counting backward from ten, engaging his trained musician's brain to dismiss it as auditory hallucination born of fatigue or stress. But music was not subject to logic like that, nor could he force the silence back into submission when the universe itself seemed determined to play a prank on him tonight.

He closed his eyes and let the C-sharp wash over him, wondering if maybe time had folded in on itself here inside this cramped apartment, creating an echo of some past performance lost forever or perhaps one that never happened at all. The note grew louder as he listened, swelling with a volume that made no sense physically but felt entirely right emotionally; it was the sound of absence giving voice to presence, a ghost playing out loud in his living room without permission from anyone alive today. Elias reached for his headphones and plugged them into an old amplifier sitting on his desk, hoping somehow to capture the frequency scientifically so he could analyze its waveform later, though he suspected even waveforms would fail here because this sound existed outside of measurable physics entirely.

Hours passed blurred together as rain continued to drum against glass while inside, only one note sustained itself endlessly in a loop that refused closure or resolution. Eventually exhaustion overtook him not from sleep but from the sheer effort required simply to remain conscious within such an impossible reality; finally he allowed himself to slip into unconsciousness with his hand still resting on keys long since released by fingers no longer present there, leaving only silence behind once more until morning brought light and questions neither answered nor asked aloud ever again.
topic: a piano tuner who hears a note nobody played
